followUps: The question about input size and constraints matters most, because it decides which algorithm is even acceptable. Situation: in a practice round I was asked to find duplicates. I asked how big the array was; the answer was 10 million numbers, so a nested loop at O(N^2) was out and I went straight to a hash set at O(N) time. Second in value is the edge-case question (empty input, negatives), since it prevents bugs I would otherwise find late.

If the interviewer says "you decide", I pick a reasonable default, say it aloud, and move on. For example: "I will assume integers, up to 100,000 elements, duplicates allowed, and I will return -1 if nothing is found. Tell me if any of that is wrong." That shows I can make a call under uncertainty, and it keeps the door open for a correction. I do not stall or ask the same question again; I write the assumptions at the top of the board so we both can see them.

I skip the brute force when it is so obvious or the problem is so standard that naming it wastes time. Example: in a round where the task was a simple binary search on a sorted array, I said in one sentence that a linear scan is O(N) and that sorted input allows O(log N), then coded the binary search. I also skip it when the interviewer says they want to focus on the optimal idea. The rule is: never skip the reasoning, only shorten it to one sentence.

Then I say so, and that is a good result, not a failure. I explain why nothing better exists, for example "every element must be read at least once, so O(N) is a lower bound, and my solution does exactly one pass." Then I move to what is left: reduce the constant factor or space, handle edge cases, and test. In one round, summing a list was the whole problem; I stated the lower bound in two sentences, coded it in four lines, and used the remaining time on tests and variants like overflow.

At about minute 3 I say exactly what I tried and where I am blocked, then ask a narrow question. I would say: "I tried a hash map on the sample [2, 7, 11, 15] with target 9 and it works for pairs, but I do not see how to handle the case where the same number appears twice. I am thinking about sorting with two pointers. Is that direction reasonable, or am I missing a property of the input?" This shows my process, saves time, and makes it easy for them to give a small nudge instead of the answer.

I keep calm by relying on a fixed routine, so I never have to improvise under stress. When my chest feels tight, I take one slow breath, write a tiny example on the board, and work through it by hand. Situation: in one mock round I froze for about 20 seconds; I said "let me do a small example", traced three numbers, and the pattern appeared. I also practised with a timer so the pressure felt familiar, and I remind myself that being stuck for a few minutes is normal and expected.

I say so politely and explain my reasoning, because blind agreement would hide my thinking. For example: "I see your point about sorting first. It would make the pairs easy, but it costs O(N log N), and I think the hash map keeps us at O(N). Can I check that on the example, and if sorting looks better after that I will switch?" Then I actually test both on the sample. If the interviewer is right, I say so and move on; if not, the test shows it without any argument.

I say that honestly and use it as a chance to go further, not to pretend it was a new idea. Example: when told "think about a stack", I replied: "I had considered that. I rejected it at first because the order of elements is not nested, but you are right it fits the matching part." Being honest builds trust, and showing I had weighed it earlier is a good sign. I never claim the idea as brand new, and I never ignore it; I then explain which trade-off I want to compare.

Three or four well-chosen tests are enough, as long as each one targets a different kind of failure. My set is: the given sample, an empty or single-element input, a case with duplicates or negatives, and a case with no answer. Example for a function that finds the maximum: [3, 9, 2] (normal), [] (empty), [-5, -1] (all negative), [7] (single). Four tests, four different risks. If time remains I add one large input to think about performance. More than that usually repeats the same risk.

At scale, I test in layers and automate. Steps: 1) unit tests for each function with edge cases, 2) property-based or randomised tests that compare my fast code to a simple brute force on thousands of small random inputs, 3) load or performance tests on realistic data sizes, 4) monitoring in production for errors and latency. In a past project I compared a rewritten routine with the old one on 50,000 random cases and found an off-by-one that handwritten tests had missed. The brute-force oracle is cheap and catches many bugs.

I keep going, politely steer the conversation, and trade a little talking time for a shorter code section. I say: "I want to make sure we have time for testing, so may I start coding the agreed approach now?" Usually an interviewer who talks a lot is giving hints or sharing context, so I listen, because it is useful. If time still runs short, I cut optional work such as polish, never the dry run. I also write my minute checkpoints at the top of the board so I notice drift early.

I scale each phase and use the extra 15 minutes where it earns the most points. For example: clarify 5, approach 9, code 20, testing 10, complexity and follow-ups 8, plus 3 for intro and 5 for my questions, which comes to 60. The extra time mostly goes to a second, harder follow-up or to deeper testing, not to slower coding. I still set checkpoints: approach agreed by about minute 18, code done by about minute 38, and I tell the interviewer so they know I am watching the clock.

With only 5 minutes left, I choose the smallest working fix and protect a short test. Steps: 1) say what is wrong with one failing input, 2) patch only that, for example adding a check for an empty list, 3) dry run the sample once, 4) state what I would improve with more time. If a patch is impossible, I explain the brute force clearly and give its complexity so I leave with a correct answer. A working, tested simple solution beats a half-written better one.

Yes, a rewrite is right when the approach is wrong at its core and a patch would only add special cases. Example: I started a greedy solution for coin change with coins [1, 3, 4] and amount 6; greedy gives 4+1+1 = 3 coins, but 3+3 = 2 coins is better. No small patch fixes that, so I switched to dynamic programming at O(amount x coins). I decide using time left: with 20 minutes I rewrite, with 5 I patch or present the brute force. I always say aloud why I am restarting.

If the interviewer is silent, I treat silence as permission to continue and keep checking in at section boundaries. I say: "I will assume this is a design for 10 million daily users and move to the API; stop me if you want a different scale." Some interviewers stay quiet on purpose to see whether I can lead. I make assumptions explicit, ask a short question at each checkpoint, and read small cues such as a nod. I do not fill the quiet with rambling; I move to the next step of my plan.

I pick the deep dive on the riskiest component, the one where the main trade-offs live or where the numbers look hardest. Example: for a URL shortener at 100 million new links per month (about 40 writes per second), the reads are the harder part, so I would dive into the key generation and the cache. I also offer the interviewer a choice: "I see two risky parts, ID generation and the read cache. Which one interests you more?" That uses their hints and shows I know where the risk is.

I stay calm and keep to the facts, restating what I know and the cost. I might say: "I understand the concern about consistency. With the numbers we set, 5,000 writes per second and one region, the single database handles it, and I would move to sharding past about 20,000." If they keep pushing, I ask what requirement they want me to weigh differently, because the disagreement is often about a hidden assumption. Then I either adjust the design under that new requirement or agree to disagree with a clear reason.

Then I admit it honestly and move to a better choice, instead of defending something weak. I say: "You are right, I picked it from habit and cannot justify it against the requirements. Let me compare the alternatives." Then I list two options and pick one using the numbers. In an earlier round I chose a message queue without a need for asynchronous work and, when asked, simply removed it and simplified the design. Interviewers value honesty and fast correction far more than a stubborn defence.

I would record myself and review it, so I have evidence rather than a feeling. Steps: 1) do a mock interview with a friend or a recorder, 2) count how often I code before asking questions and how long my silences last, 3) ask the mock interviewer to score communication on a short rubric, 4) repeat after two weeks to compare. In one review I found I had spoken for 10 seconds of every minute and was silent the rest, so I started narrating while writing. Evidence from three or four sessions is enough to see patterns.

Long silences and jumping into code are the most fixable, because they are habits, not talent. Fix them with a fixed opening script: restate, give an example, ask three questions, state the brute force, then ask "may I code?". For silence, I practise narrating small steps aloud, even simple ones like "now I am updating the pointer". Within a couple of weeks of daily practice both usually improve. Harder to fix are gaps in knowledge, such as not explaining complexity, which need real study.

I would reject output that is wrong, unclear, or that I cannot explain. Checks: an invented API or method that does not exist, a loop that mutates a list while iterating it, a missing empty-input case, or the wrong complexity. Example: the assistant gave a solution that used a nested loop for finding duplicates, O(N^2), when I knew a set would give O(N), so I rejected it and asked for the set version. If I cannot trace the code on a small example, I do not keep it. Running it and adding my own test is the final gate.

I would not claim it as my own idea; I would explain it honestly by reading it as a reviewer. Steps: 1) state what the code is meant to do in one sentence, 2) walk through it on a tiny example, such as [1, 2, 2] with a duplicate check, 3) name the data structure and the complexity, 4) point out one risk or one thing I changed. If a part is unclear, I say so and either simplify it or ask the interviewer. Code that I cannot explain is code I should not submit.

If I have no ideas, I use a short checklist so I still add value. I can talk about complexity and why it cannot be improved, test cases I have not run, how the code behaves with input too big for memory, or how I would make it readable and add logging. Example: after solving two-sum, I could say "for a stream of numbers I would keep the set between calls". If nothing comes, I simply ask: "Is there an area you would like me to look at?" Asking is better than silence or random code.

Not as a request, because it sounds like I want to stop. Instead I say "I believe this is complete; let me summarise the complexity and what else I could check", and let the interviewer end or extend the round. They know the schedule and may have a follow-up ready, so finishing early often just leads to a harder question, which is a chance to show more. I never end by saying "that is all" with 12 minutes left; I stay in the problem and keep showing depth.

If I notice only after the interview, I accept it, learn from it, and where it makes sense send a brief, honest follow-up. Steps: 1) write the mistake and the right answer down while it is fresh, 2) add it to my list of recurring errors, 3) if the recruiter allows, send a two-line note: "After the call I realised my complexity claim for part 2 was wrong; it is O(N log N), not O(N)." That is rare and optional but shows honesty. Mostly the value is the lesson for the next round, so I practise that exact case.

I keep a mistake log and turn each entry into a checklist item. For each error I note the cause (rushed, assumed, did not test) and a one-line rule. Example: after three off-by-one bugs I added "check the loop bounds on a 1-element input" to my final check. I review the list before mock interviews and re-do the same problem a week later without notes to confirm the fix. Repeating the problem under time pressure is what makes the habit stick, not just reading the note.
